query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy nanoalloys for high‐temperature applications, the high configurational entropy that stabilizes a single-phase solid solution works in tandem with a refined (nanoscale) grain structure to suppress elemental segregation and nucleation of deleterious phases (including non‐protective oxides). This synergy governs both structural and chemical stability by reducing the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation and minimizing the sites for localized oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A uniformly mixed high‐entropy nanoalloy (e.g., a refractory or multi‐principal element alloy produced via rapid solidification or laser‐based additive manufacturing) exhibiting a nanocrystalline grain structure with near–equiatomic proportions of at least five elements.
generation.intervention: Conduct a series of controlled high-temperature annealing experiments on samples of identical nominal composition but with different average grain sizes – one set engineered to be highly refined (nanoscale, <100 nm) and a comparison set with coarser grains.
generation.conditions: Isothermal annealing at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1100 °C) under controlled oxygen partial pressures (to mimic service atmospheres) and for durations sufficient for potential phase separation and oxidation to occur.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale grain boundaries and the overall interfacial energy landscape that influences diffusion and elemental segregation.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy inherently lowers the driving force for phase separation, while a finer grain structure distributes potential reactive sites more uniformly. This promotes the formation of a coherent, self-healing protective oxide (or minimizes deleterious oxide growth) and limits local chemical fluctuations, jointly enhancing structural retention and chemical resistance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarser-grained counterparts, the nanocrystalline high-entropy alloys will retain a single-phase solid solution with minimal elemental segregation after high-temperature exposure and will exhibit lower oxidation rates (e.g., lower weight gain due to protective rather than disruptive oxide formation).
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained or partially homogenized high-entropy alloys of the same composition that are more prone to local elemental segregation and phase decomposition upon high-temperature annealing.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold for high-entropy alloys in which the combined effect of high mixing entropy and a sufficiently refined microstructure is maintained; however, if processing defects or compositional inhomogeneities dominate, or if the protective oxide formed is not self-limiting, the behavior may deviate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements in phase and oxidation stability is uncertain due to potential influences of minor compositional variations and processing-induced defects. Quantitative differences in oxidation kinetics and phase decomposition boundaries will require further experimental delineation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of high-entropy nanoalloy samples of identical composition but differing in average grain size (one set nanocrystalline, one set coarser-grained). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature annealing conditions (e.g., 900 °C, controlled oxygen partial pressure, for 100–200 hours). Characterize the phase composition by X-ray diffraction (XRD), microstructure and grain boundary chemistry by SEM/TEM with EDS, and measure oxidation kinetics via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) or weight gain measurements.
measurements: SEM/TEM imaging for grain size and microstructural changes
EDS mapping to detect elemental segregation at grain boundaries
TGA or weight gain analysis to quantify oxidation rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanocrystalline samples do not show significantly improved retention of the single-phase structure and reduced oxidation (i.e., if oxidation rates and phase decomposition patterns are statistically indistinguishable from or worse than those observed in the coarse-grained samples), then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy combined with nanoscale grain structure governs enhanced stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations.
